To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.

# Project Kestrel — Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter

Below is my critical review of the Seller's draft. I've grouped issues by severity, with my reasoning and the pushback for each. These documents are the counterparty's draft — every position is drafted to favour the Seller, so treat nothing as "agreed" simply because it is labelled that way.

---

## A. Most serious issues (price / deal certainty)

### 1. Riverlark debt — "release following Completion" breaks the debt-free/cash-free deal
**Seller position:** The ~AUD 3.2m Riverlark facility "will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion" (Update cl. 2/7; Disclosure §3 confirms it is NOT repaid and no discharge is included).

**Why this hurts us:** Our baseline is **debt-free/cash-free**. In a cash-free/debt-free deal, financial debt must be repaid at or before Completion and security discharged *as a condition of* Completion — not afterward. "Following Completion" means we would own a company still carrying AUD 3.2m of debt and secured charges, relying on a seller promise post-closing. If Seller fails to deliver the discharge, we are an unsecured creditor chasing them. This is effectively a ~AUD 3.2m price shift onto us.

**Push back:** Repayment and discharge of the Riverlark facility must be a **Completion deliverable / condition precedent**, with a deed of release and discharge of security (and ASIC/PPSR release) handed over at Completion. Alternatively, the amount is deducted from the funds flow and paid directly to Riverlark at Completion. Do not accept a post-Completion undertaking.

### 2. Funds flow excludes the DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000)
**Seller position:** The AUD 420k Completion bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" and not itemised in the funds flow (Update; Disclosure §5).

**Why this hurts us:** These bonuses are triggered *by Completion* and are conditional on continued employment — i.e., they are liabilities of the **Company** that crystallise on the deal we are doing. If they sit with the Company, we pay them. Calling them "a matter for the Seller" without a mechanism makes that assertion meaningless. Worse, §5 flags that **payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs** are unaddressed — so the true exposure is >AUD 420k.

**Push back:** Either (a) these are a Seller obligation discharged at Completion out of Seller proceeds (reflected in the funds flow), or (b) they are treated as Completion debt / a specific indemnity (grossed up for super, payroll tax and on-costs). Get the number quantified and allocated. Do not leave it as a bare assertion.

### 3. Bluefen change-control consent — "deemed satisfied on delivery" is circular
**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours; consent "treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" (Update cl. 3/6.3). Disclosure §2 confirms **no consent and no evidence the conditions in cl. 11.3 are satisfied**.

**Why this hurts us:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue — a material customer with a change-of-control clause. "Satisfied on delivery of consent" is circular drafting: it tells us nothing about *whether* consent will be obtained, and cl. 11.3 **conditions** may make the consent conditional/ineffective. "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak standard. If we complete without a valid, unconditional consent, Bluefen could terminate ~30% of revenue post-Completion.

**Push back:** Obtaining a valid, **unconditional** Bluefen consent (satisfying the cl. 11.3 conditions) should be a **condition precedent to Completion**, with a "best endeavours" obligation on the Seller. If Seller resists CP status, we need a specific indemnity / price adjustment for loss of Bluefen within a defined period post-Completion. Confirm whether cl. 11.3 conditions are capable of satisfaction.

---

## B. Risk-allocation provisions skewed to Seller

### 4. Fundamental / title warranties capped and time-limited like general warranties
**Seller position:** "For administrative simplicity," capacity and title warranties get the **same 20% cap and 18-month limit** as general warranties (Update "Fundamental/Title").

**Why this hurts us:** This is the single most important limitation point. **Title and capacity are fundamental** — if the Seller doesn't actually own 100% of the shares, we get nothing we bargained for. Market practice is that fundamental/title warranties are capped at **100% of the purchase price** and have a **long limitation period** (often 6–7 years, aligned to tax). "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap our most important protection at AUD 4.8m. Note also §10 flatly says title rests only on the share register and Seller has not verified anything for us.

**Push back:** Reject. Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority) must be capped at **100% of price (AUD 24m)** with a limitation period of at least 6–7 years. **Tax warranties** should run to the end of the statutory assessment/amendment period (not 18 months — see item 9).

### 5. General liability cap of 20% / AUD 4.8m
**Seller position:** 20% cap.

**Why this hurts us:** 20% is at the low end for a privately-held target of this size, especially given the concentration risk (Bluefen 30%) and the open incidents. Caps of 25–50% are common.

**Push back:** Negotiate the general cap up (target 30–50%), and carve out the fundamental/tax/specific-indemnity items from this cap entirely (item 4).

### 6. 18-month general limitation + "applies to all Claims unless stated otherwise"
**Seller position:** 18 months for general claims, and the limitation "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (Update cl. 12.3/13).

**Why this hurts us:** 18 months is short — it may not survive a full audit cycle to surface warranty breaches. More dangerously, the **default sweep** ("applies to all Claims unless expressly stated") is a drafting trap: it would silently pull **tax, fundamental, and specific indemnities** into the 18-month window unless we affirmatively carve each one out. The burden should be the other way round.

**Push back:** (a) Extend general period to **24 months** (through two audit cycles). (b) **Reverse the default**: limitations apply only to general warranty claims; fundamental, tax, and specific-indemnity claims have their own longer periods. Reject the "applies to all unless expressly stated otherwise" sweep.

### 7. Limitations / exclusive-remedy / non-reliance "apply to all Claims of any nature"
**Seller position:** cl. 9.3/12.8/20.5 apply to all Claims of any nature.

**Why this hurts us:** A blanket exclusive-remedy and non-reliance regime applying to "all Claims of any nature" would attempt to exclude **fraud** and specific indemnities. Under NSW law you cannot contract out of liability for your own fraud, and attempting to do so is a red flag.

**Push back:** Carve out **fraud, wilful concealment, and the specific indemnities** from all limitation, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions. Fundamental/title/tax claims should also sit outside the exclusive-remedy construct to the extent needed.

### 8. Buyer knowledge / data-room "deemed knowledge" bar (cl. 8.3) + general disclosure sweep
**Seller position:** No claim for anything the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge," *including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records* (Update cl. 8.3). Combined with Disclosure §§1.1–1.2 blanket-disclosing the **entire data room** and public registers.

**Why this hurts us:** This is a double mechanism to gut the warranties:
- **Constructive/"discoverable" knowledge** — not just what we actually knew, but anything we *could* have found — is far too broad and effectively transfers all diligence risk to us.
- **Blanket "deemed disclosure" of everything in the data room** means any warranty is qualified by whatever is buried anywhere in DD-002–DD-012, even if not fairly disclosed against a specific warranty.

**Push back:** (a) Knowledge limited to **actual knowledge** of a named deal team, not constructive/"discoverable" knowledge, and no deemed knowledge of advisers' files. (b) Disclosure must be **fair and specific** — "fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope" — not a blanket data-room dump. Reject general disclosure of the entire data room and public registers as a qualification to the warranties. Note §1.4 also disclaims that anything disclosed admits liability/materiality — fine for them, but it underscores that "disclosure" here is being used as a shield, not information.

### 9. Tax warranties folded into the "general regime"
**Seller position:** Tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime above."

**Why this hurts us:** Tax exposure can arise years after Completion (ATO amendment periods). An 18-month limit and 20% cap on tax is inadequate.

**Push back:** Separate **tax deed/indemnity** with limitation tied to the statutory amendment period (typically up to 7 years) and outside the general cap. IP warranties — see Ironquay below.

---

## C. Specific disclosed risks needing targeted protection

### 10. Ironquay IP — indemnity too narrow (title to deliverables at risk)
**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to the specific SOW3 payment is "adequate" (cl. 11.1). Disclosure §4: DD-004 cl. 7.3 conditions **transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**; AUD 180k is recorded open; **no proof of payment or assignment** in the data room.

**Why this hurts us:** This is not merely a payment dispute — it is an **IP title** problem. Until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials may **not have passed to the Company**. The Company could be using/selling deliverables it doesn't own. Capping the indemnity at "the SOW3 payment" (AUD 180k) ignores the real exposure: loss of rights to use the IP, customer claims, re-development cost. The data room also doesn't even verify the amount outstanding (§4).

**Push back:** (a) Confirm SOW3 fees fully paid and obtain a **confirmatory assignment / written confirmation that title has vested** — ideally as a Completion deliverable. (b) The indemnity must cover **loss of/challenge to IP title and consequential loss**, not just the SOW3 fee. (c) Specific IP warranty that the Company owns or is licensed to all material IP used in the business.

### 11. DD-006 export / privacy incident — understated
**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter... not expected to be material" (cl. 4.6/Sch 6). Disclosure §6: download link sent to an unintended external email; ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); scope/access/notification all unresolved.

**Why this hurts us:** This is a **potential notifiable data breach** under the Privacy Act (NDB scheme). 1,240 individuals' personal information disclosed to an unintended recipient is not self-evidently immaterial. Exposure includes OAIC notification obligations, potential regulatory action, remediation and reputational harm — and the investigation is explicitly **incomplete**, so the Seller's "not material" characterisation is premature and self-serving.

**Push back:** (a) Specific **indemnity** covering all losses, regulatory penalties, notification/remediation costs arising from the DD-006 incident, uncapped by the general cap. (b) Interim CP: Seller to complete the investigation and provide a written assessment of scope and notification requirements before Completion. (c) Warranty of compliance with privacy/data-protection laws, with this matter specifically disclosed and indemnified rather than buried.

### 12. Mossvale (DD-009) and Office lease (DD-007) — consent/notification on change of control
**Seller position:** Disclosure §7 (lease notification not characterised as requiring consent) and §9 (Mossvale assignment restriction said not to be triggered merely by a share sale).

**Why this hurts us:** These are drafted to downplay change-of-control triggers. A **share sale** can still trigger a contractual change-of-control or notification clause even though legal ownership of assets doesn't change. We must read the **actual clauses**, not the Seller's gloss. Failure to notify the landlord could breach the lease; a triggered Mossvale restriction could affect a contract.

**Push back:** Review DD-007 and DD-009 clauses directly. Where a notification or consent is triggered by change of control, require it as a pre-Completion step or specific warranty/indemnity. Add a general warranty that **no material contract contains a change-of-control right that is triggered by the transaction** (with disclosed exceptions handled specifically).

### 13. Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330k)
**Seller position:** Three AUD 110k renewals are "ordinary-course operating costs." Disclosure §8 admits it does **not** state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course — and flags they should be "read together."

**Why this hurts us:** AUD 330k aggregate is material. The "read together" note suggests possible **structuring to stay under individual thresholds**. If these are new/committed spend outside the ordinary course, they affect value and may breach the ordinary-course covenant between signing and Completion.

**Push back:** Obtain the three contracts; confirm whether committed, terminable, and genuinely ordinary course. If committed non-ordinary-course spend, reflect in price/leakage or require as a conduct-of-business consent item.

---

## D. Thresholds (item for completeness)

### 14. De minimis AUD 25k / basket AUD 250k, excess-only recovery
**Seller position:** cl. 12.2 — AUD 25k de minimis, AUD 250k basket, recover only the excess.

**Assessment:** On a AUD 24m deal these are broadly within market range. The **excess-only ("deductible") basket** favours the Seller versus a "first-dollar/tipping" basket. This is a secondary negotiating point — I'd push for a tipping basket or at least ensure the de minimis and basket **do not apply** to fundamental, tax, and specific-indemnity claims.

---

## Summary of Recommendations

**Deal-blocking / price items (push hardest):**
1. **Riverlark debt (AUD 3.2m):** repayment + discharge of security as a **Completion condition/deliverable**, not post-Completion. 
2. **Bluefen consent (30% of revenue):** valid, unconditional consent as a **condition precedent**; fallback specific indemnity for loss of the customer. 
3. **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs):** quantify and allocate to Seller via funds flow or treat as debt/specific indemnity grossed up for super/payroll tax.

**Risk-allocation (non-negotiable protections):**
4. **Fundamental/title/capacity warranties:** 100% cap (AUD 24m), 6–7 year limitation — reject "administrative simplicity." 
5. **Tax:** separate deed/indemnity, limitation tied to statutory period, outside general cap. 
6. **Reverse the limitation default:** limitations apply to general warranties only; carve out fundamental, tax, and specific indemnities. Extend general period to 24 months. 
7. **Fraud and specific indemnities carved out** of all caps, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions. 
8. **Knowledge/disclosure:** actual knowledge of named individuals only (no "discoverable"/constructive knowledge); disclosure must be **fair and specific**, not a blanket data-room/public-register sweep. 
9. **General cap:** push from 20% toward 30–50%.

**Specific indemnities to secure (uncapped by general cap):**
10. **Ironquay IP:** confirm SOW3 paid + confirmatory assignment; indemnity covering loss of IP title and consequential loss, plus an IP ownership warranty. 
11. **DD-006 privacy incident:** specific indemnity for notification/regulatory/remediation losses; complete investigation pre-Completion; privacy-compliance warranty. 
12. **Change-of-control:** review DD-007 (lease) and DD-009 (Mossvale) clauses directly; add a no-change-of-control-trigger warranty. 
13. **Sandbar renewals (AUD 330k):** obtain contracts; confirm ordinary-course/terminable status; address as leakage or conduct item.

**Lower priority:** 
14. Thresholds broadly market; push for a tipping basket and ensure thresholds don't apply to fundamental/tax/indemnity claims.

**Overarching theme:** The Seller's package systematically (a) defers hard obligations (Riverlark, Bluefen) to post-Completion or soft endeavours, (b) flattens our strongest protections (title/tax) down to weak general-warranty levels, and (c) uses broad "deemed knowledge" + "general disclosure" drafting to neutralise the warranties. Each of these should be resisted. I'd also note we should independently verify title (§10 confirms Seller has done nothing beyond pointing at the share register) and re-run PPSR searches for the Riverlark security before Completion.

Want me to turn this into a mark-up/issues list in a table, or draft specific clause language for the priority items?

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to the specific SOW3 payment is "adequate" (cl. 11.1). Disclosure §4: DD-004 cl. 7.3 conditions **transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**; AUD 180k is recorded open; **no proof of payment or assignment** in the data room.

**Why this hurts us:** This is not merely a payment dispute — it is an **IP title** problem. Until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials may **not have passed to the Company**. The Company could be using/selling deliverables it doesn't own. Capping the indemnity at "the SOW3 payment" (AUD 180k) ignores the real exposure: loss of rights to use the IP, customer claims, re-development cost. The data room also doesn't even verify the amount outstanding (§4).

**Push back:** (a) Confirm SOW3 fees fully paid and obtain a **confirmatory assignment / written confirmation that title has vested** — ideally as a Completion deliverable. (b) The indemnity must cover **loss of/challenge to IP title and consequential loss**, not just the SOW3 fee. (c) Specific IP warranty that the Company owns or is licensed to all material IP used in the business.

### 11. DD-006 export / privacy incident — understated
**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter... not expected to be material" (cl. 4.6/Sch 6). Disclosure §6: download link sent to an unintended external email; ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); scope/access/notification all unresolved.

**Why this hurts us:** This is a **potential notifiable data breach** under the Privacy Act (NDB scheme). 1,240 individuals' personal information disclosed to an unintended recipient is not self-evidently immaterial. Exposure includes OAIC notification obligations, potential regulatory action, remediation and reputational harm — and the investigation is explicitly **incomplete**, so the Seller's "not material" characterisation is premature and self-serving.

**Push back:** (a) Specific **indemnity** covering all losses, regulatory penalties, notification/remediation costs arising from the DD-006 incident, uncapped by the general cap. (b) Interim CP: Seller to complete the investigation and provide a written assessment of scope and notification requirements before Completion. (c) Warranty of compliance with privacy/data-protection laws, with this matter specifically disclosed and indemnified rather than buried.

### 12. Mossvale (DD-009) and Office lease (DD-007) — consent/notification on change of control
**Seller position:** Disclosure §7 (lease notification not characterised as requiring consent) and §9 (Mossvale assignment restriction said not to be triggered merely by a share sale).

**Why this hurts us:** These are drafted to downplay change-of-control triggers. A **share sale** can still trigger a contractual change-of-control or notification clause even though legal ownership of assets doesn't change. We must read the **actual clauses**, not the Seller's gloss. Failure to notify the landlord could breach the lease; a triggered Mossvale restriction could affect a contract.

**Push back:** Review DD-007 and DD-009 clauses directly. Where a notification or consent is triggered by change of control, require it as a pre-Completion step or specific warranty/indemnity. Add a general warranty that **no material contract contains a change-of-control right that is triggered by the transaction** (with disclosed exceptions handled specifically).

### 13. Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330k)
**Seller position:** Three AUD 110k renewals are "ordinary-course operating costs." Disclosure §8 admits it does **not** state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course — and flags they should be "read together."

**Why this hurts us:** AUD 330k aggregate is material. The "read together" note suggests possible **structuring to stay under individual thresholds**. If these are new/committed spend outside the ordinary course, they affect value and may breach the ordinary-course covenant between signing and Completion.

**Push back:** Obtain the three contracts; confirm whether committed, terminable, and genuinely ordinary course. If committed non-ordinary-course spend, reflect in price/leakage or require as a conduct-of-business consent item.

## D. Thresholds (item for completeness)

### 14. De minimis AUD 25k / basket AUD 250k, excess-only recovery
**Seller position:** cl. 12.2 — AUD 25k de minimis, AUD 250k basket, recover only the excess.

**Assessment:** On a AUD 24m deal these are broadly within market range. The **excess-only ("deductible") basket** favours the Seller versus a "first-dollar/tipping" basket. This is a secondary negotiating point — I'd push for a tipping basket or at least ensure the de minimis and basket **do not apply** to fundamental, tax, and specific-indemnity claims.
